title: Carpets and tiles
hook: prayer rugs, Persian carpets, Iznik tiles

segments.voice: Yesterday, gardens with running water, and the jannah they point toward. Your line was: under which rivers flow. Did you drink a glass of water slowly? Day one thousand ten.

At prayer time, in the corner of an office, someone unrolls a small rectangle of cloth, smooths a wrinkle with one hand, checks the direction, and steps onto it. A minute ago this was the spot by the printer. Now it's a place of prayer. Far away, in an old mosque in Istanbul, the walls are covered in tiles: deep blue, turquoise, and a red like a ripe tomato, painted with tulips and carnations. Underfoot, a carpet. On the walls, a garden in glazed clay. Cloth and clay. Today: mihrab.
screen: `A RUG UNROLLED BY THE PRINTER.` → `A MOSQUE WALL OF TILES.` → `CLOTH AND CLAY.`

segments.voice: Start with the rug. A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Sahih al-Bukhari, says the earth has been made for him a place of prayer, and pure. Any clean ground will do. So a prayer rug isn't required. It does a quieter job: it marks off a clean patch of floor, and it lets someone carry a place of prayer rolled up under one arm. Another hadith in al-Bukhari mentions the Prophet praying on a small mat. On many prayer rugs, the weaver puts an arch at one end, the shape of the mihrab, the niche in a mosque wall that shows the direction of prayer. Lay the rug the right way, and the little arch points where to face. Then there are the great carpets, Persian and Turkish and more, knotted by hand. Some are woven as gardens, yesterday's channels and all: a garden you can keep on the floor. The Qur'an's own picture of paradise has carpets in it. In Pickthall's translation: "And silken carpets spread." Now the tiles. In the town of Iznik, in Turkey, potters made tiles in white, cobalt blue and turquoise, with a red that sits up slightly from the glaze. The Ottomans lined mosques with them, so tulips climb the walls around the people praying. One more thing, because it gets told a lot: people say weavers leave a deliberate mistake in every carpet, because only God is perfect. It's a story people tell. There's no sure source behind it, and a weaver's mistakes can arrive on their own. Woven prayer.
screen: `ANY CLEAN GROUND WILL DO.` · `AN ARCH THAT POINTS THE WAY.` · `A GARDEN ON THE FLOOR.` · `TULIPS CLIMB THE IZNIK TILES.` · then, large: `WOVEN PRAYER.`

segments.voice: The practice: touch a woven thing. A rug, a scarf, a blanket, the sleeve of what you're wearing. Settle, and breathe. Run your fingers slowly across it. Feel where the threads cross, and cross again. Someone put every one of those crossings there, by hand or with a machine that someone built and tended. Think about those hands for a moment. If you pray, you can thank God for them. If you don't, just thank them, quietly, wherever they are. The bell holds the time.
Mihrab, the niche that shows the direction of prayer: its arch is woven into prayer rugs, and tiled gardens of tulips climb the walls around it. Today's word.
Your line: woven prayer. Today, notice one handmade thing you use, and handle it with a little more care. Day one thousand ten.

howItsDone: At home or at work, a Muslim may pray on a prayer rug laid toward Mecca, though any clean place is enough; mosque floors are commonly carpeted, and some Ottoman mosques are lined with Iznik tiles.
